name: High-quality coprime abc triples
description: construct() -> [a,b,c], positive Python integers <=1000000000000, a<=b, a+b=c, gcd(a,b)=1. Maximize log(c)/log(rad(a*b*c)). The radical is the product of DISTINCT prime factors and is independently factored exactly; only the logarithmic score uses floating arithmetic. Search coprime positive triples a+b=c with c<=10^12, maximizing log(c)/log(rad(abc)). Finite high quality cannot disprove the conjecture, which allows finitely many exceptions at each exponent. The optimum is Reyssat's quality 1.62991 for 2 + 3^10*109 = 23^5; complete tables of high-quality triples show nothing better below 10^20, so this is a rediscovery task.

JSP-000010; pinned discovery record, independently paraphrased. Source wording and paper-specific differences are explained in limitations.

state_of_the_art.statement: Reyssat's triple 2 + 3^10·109 = 23^5 (c = 6,436,343) has quality 1.62991. De Smit's complete tables of triples with quality at least 1.4 and at most twenty digits, surveyed by Martin and Miao, contain nothing of higher quality, so it is the maximum for c <= 10^12.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Construct and understand integer triples with unusually small radical relative to height.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The abc conjecture of Masser and Oesterlé is a central open problem in number theory; triples of high quality are the extremal examples that test it, and finding them is the main goal of the cited paper.

papers.primary_goal: Find abc triples of high quality, i.e. good examples for the abc and Szpiro conjectures, by lattice reduction.

science_relevance.reason: A problem-focused primary paper (Tim Dokchitser, Journal of Number Theory 107 (2004), DOI 10.1016/j.jnt.2004.02.003) is devoted to finding high-quality abc triples, the quantity this task maximizes. No novelty claim is implied.
science_relevance.verification_basis: Author abstract, arXiv math/0307322: the LLL algorithm applied to prime powers finds good examples for the ABC and Szpiro conjectures. The Martin and Miao survey (p.3) defines the logarithmic quality used here.
